question: Can textual feedback from LLMs be backpropagated through a computation graph of LLM calls and tools, PyTorch-style, to optimize prompts, solutions and other text variables of compound AI systems with one general framework?
hypothesis: Current state-of-the-art LLMs can reason about individual components and subtasks of a system well enough that their natural-language criticism works as a general-purpose gradient.
contributions: TextGrad, an autograd-style framework (Variables, Functions, TGD optimizer, tg.sum) with PyTorch syntax, open-sourced
Instance optimization results on LeetCode Hard code, GPQA and MMLU subsets
Prompt optimization results for gpt-3.5-turbo on Object Counting, Word Sorting, GSM8k versus DSPy
Proof-of-concept molecule design (58 DOCKSTRING targets) and radiotherapy plan hyperparameter optimization

method.summary: Each AI system is a computation graph of text variables. A backward LLM call per edge produces natural-language feedback ('textual gradients') from successors, concatenated over successors; a Textual Gradient Descent (TGD) LLM call rewrites the variable from its value plus feedback. Used for instance optimization (test-time refinement of a solution) and prompt optimization (minibatch system-prompt tuning).
method.task: Optimizing text variables (code, answers, system prompts, SMILES strings, planning hyperparameters) in compound LLM systems

prompts.text: You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). ... If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback. {GLOSSARY}
prompts.where: Appendix A.3 (abridged with '...' in the examples sentence)

prompts.text: You are part of an optimization system that improves text (i.e., variable). You will be asked to creatively and critically improve prompts, solutions to problems, code, or any other text-based variable. You will receive some feedback, and use the feedback to improve the variable. The feedback may be noisy, identify what is important and what is correct. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. This is very important: You MUST give your response by sending the improved variable between <IMPROVED_VARIABLE> improved variable </IMPROVED_VARIABLE> tags. The text you send between the tags will directly replace the variable. {GLOSSARY}

Below is a multi-choice question and a prediction. You are a critical and creative scientist. Your job is to investigate the prediction. Critically go through reasoning steps, and see if there is a reason why the prediction could be incorrect. Use the Janusian Process, think about whether alternative answers could be true. Question: {Question} Answer by the language model: {Solution}

You are an intelligent assistant used as an evaluator, and part of an optimization system. You will analyze a code implementation for a coding problem and unit test results. The code will be tested with harder tests, so do not just check if the code passes the provided tests. Think about the correctness of the code and its performance in harder test cases. Give very concise feedback. Investigate the code problem and the provided implementation. For each failed unit test case, start analyzing it by saying "The code did not pass this test because...". Explain why the current implementation is not getting the expected output. Do not provide a revised implementation. Carefully suggest why there are issues with the code and provide feedback. {Test-time Instruction} **The coding problem:** {Problem} **Code generated that must be evaluated for correctness and runtime performance** {Code} **The test results:** {Local test Results}

prompts.purpose: Multiple choice answering template and constraint
prompts.text: Answer the following multiple choice question. The last line of your response should be of the following format: 'Answer: $LETTER' (without quotes) where LETTER is one of ABCD. Think step by step before answering.

Below is a question from a question-answering task, the ground truth answer, and reasoning with the final prediction. Is the final prediction correct, i.e. the same as the ground truth answer? Say only 1 (yes) or 0 (no). Return your response within <ACCURACY> </ACCURACY> tags.

Given a docking and a druglikeness score, and a molecule as a SMILES string provide a short criticism to improve the druglikeness of this molecule and its binding affinity with the protein {protein_name}. For docking, lower is better (less than -10 is considered good) and for druglikeness, 1 is the best and 0 is the worst (greater than 0.8 is considered good). In terms of prioritization, the docking score is {vina_qed_ratio} times as important as the druglikeness score. Make sure your criticism is very succinct and to the point.
Here are the past iterations of this variable: <PAST_ITERATIONS>{past_values}</PAST_ITERATIONS>

limits: Authors say molecule and plan results are in silico proof of concept; experimental and clinical assessment is out of scope
Authors list stability improvements (variance reduction, adaptive gradients, self-verification) as future work, implying the optimization is unstable
Authors note reliability of constraint following drops with many constraints
No variance, seeds or significance tests for QA and prompt-optimization tables; Table 3 test sets are 100 examples for two tasks
LeetCode dataset was re-extracted and may not match Reflexion's; zero-shot printed as 0.26 in Table 1 but 23% in text
Prompt optimization is gated by validation accuracy and compared to a DSPy run configured by the authors
Cost and latency are not reported although each iteration needs several gpt-4o calls (up to n gradient calls for n edges)
Temperatures for TextGrad's own calls and max tokens are not stated
gpt-4o and gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 are dated API models; results may not reproduce

terms.definition: natural language feedback from an LLM describing how a variable should change to improve the downstream objective
optimizer that asks an LLM to produce a new variable given the current value and its gradients
treating a solution to a single problem as the optimization variable, improved at test time
finding a prompt that improves an LLM's performance across multiple queries for a task

code.snippet:
system_prompt = tg.Variable("You are a helpful language model. Think step by step.", requires_grad=True, role_description="system prompt to the language model")
model = tg.BlackboxLLM(system_prompt=system_prompt)
optimizer = tg.TextualGradientDescent(parameters=[system_prompt])
for iteration in range(max_iterations):
    batch_x, batch_y = next(train_loader)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    responses = model(batch_x)
    losses = [loss_fn(response, y) for (response, y) in zip(responses, batch_y)]
    total_loss = tg.sum(losses)
    total_loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
